extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent litigation and prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards governing (A) when and how letters-patent may be repealed (grounds, procedure, who may sue, effects of repeal) and (B) how letters-patent are to be interpreted (who decides, rules of construction, evidentiary limits, liberal construction in favor of inventor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents repealable at common law in three classes
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law a grant by the sovereign was revocable in three classes of cases: (1) where the same subject-matter had been previously granted; (2) where the grant had been procured by fraud; (3) where the subject-matter of the grant could not legally be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under U.S. law the first class has been modified and provided with special remedy; our law sustains the one granted to the first and true inventor and repeals others. The common-law presumption that the first patent is conclusive has been displaced; conflicts are resolved to protect the first and true inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings for repeal necessary when patent obtained by fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent procured by fraud not only confers no just rights on the patentee but, while it exists, constitutes an unwarrantable limitation on the sovereign power; such patents should be repealed in the interest of the whole people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals cannot adequately redress the public injury (patent is a sovereign grant and cannot be collaterally attacked), governmental interference (suit by the United States) is required to annul patents obtained by fraud. The public owes it to itself to revoke patents procured by false suggestions or concealments amounting to fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings for repeal sometimes necessary where subject-matter cannot lawfully be patented
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the grant is of a subject-matter which by law cannot be granted, the government has authority to revoke the grant; such cases are comparatively rare but may demand interference in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinarily patent-office proceedings and defenses in infringement suits suffice to protect against unlawful patents; but where a patent's invalidity is established by repeated court decisions and it is being used oppressively, the government should withdraw the appearance of authority by immediate and final revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding for repeal is by bill in equity in the name of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings to repeal an unlawful patent of the second (fraud) or third (unpatentable subject) classes are by a bill in chancery in the name of the government or its Attorney-General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such proceedings are instituted with great caution; only the Attorney-General (in the name of the United States) may maintain a bill to limit or repeal a patent. The Attorney-General must be satisfied that sufficient grounds exist before using the government's name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney-General control and prerequisites for instituting repeal suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attorney-General must be satisfied that sufficient grounds exist for submitting the question to the courts; if in doubt he may be guided by the opinion of the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases of alleged fraudulent procurement he may act at the instigation of a private party, but not where the matters urged could be used by the relator in his own defense when sued. Proceedings remain under his control and may be prosecuted or discontinued at his discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and judgment upon a bill for repeal (chancery practice and standards of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a bill in equity the process, pleadings, hearing, and decrees follow the usual course of chancery proceedings; all persons to be affected by the repeal must be made parties, and the grounds of the repeal must be established beyond reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgment in favor of the public extinguishes the patent and all rights accruing under it, even in the hands of an innocent bona fide purchaser; the owners must surrender the patent to the Patent Office for cancellation. Costs may be decreed against owners whose false suggestions led to issuance, but not against owners not party to the fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent may be repealed for fraud even if some owners are innocent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent will be repealed on account of the fraud of the patentee when he was not the true inventor, although his co-owner or assignee was not a party to the fraud but was a bona fide assignee for valuable consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs, however, may be decreed against the fraudulent party but not against an owner who was not a party to the fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and scope of the patent monopoly determined by legal interpretation of the letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The character and scope of a patent privilege is determined by the construction given to the letters-patent; the patented invention is the art or instrument which the patent really describes and claims according to its true legal interpretation, not necessarily what the inventor thought he discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rights of the patentee and the public's rights depend on the meaning which the law attaches to the language of the patent; interpreting letters-patent imposes vast responsibility on the tribunal and demands industrial skill and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of letters-patent is a matter of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims are valid or invalid, whether they embrace a given invention, and what the actual nature of the invention is are questions of law for the court to be decided upon inspection of the instrument itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be received to explain technical terms or facts necessary to comprehend the language, but such extraneous evidence cannot directly control the legal construction. The court must declare the meaning; the jury may decide factual questions (e.g., sufficiency of the specification as enabling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert testimony limited to explaining technical matters, not to fix construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When technical terms or qualities of substances or operations are unknown to the judge, testimony of witnesses may be received upon these subjects to aid comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such testimony aids the court's understanding but the actual interpretation of the patent remains the court's legal duty; opinions of patentees or experts are not binding on the court as to legal construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of confiding patent interpretation to courts (judicial construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting interpretation of letters-patent to courts as a matter of law gives the inventor a permanent definition of his rights; judicial interpretation is reviewable and less likely to be erroneous than a jury's view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge, by training and discipline, is more likely to interpret complicated written instruments correctly; his decisions are open to appellate review, unlike jury verdicts which do not state reasons and are not analyzable in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: patents to be liberally construed in favor of the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental rule requires that a patent and each of its parts be liberally interpreted in favor of the patentee; patents are property and every presumption of law supports their validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubtful points should be resolved so as to support the patentee's claims; the specification should be read in a liberal spirit and, if possible, construed to sustain the patent rather than defeat it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction consists in giving words legitimate meanings to reflect the true invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal construction interprets terms so as to protect the actual invention: give each word or phrase one of its legitimate meanings that makes the whole claim or description correspond most accurately with the essential characteristics of the true invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach recognizes that claims and descriptions are often unskilfully drawn; courts should apply meanings that effectuate the intention of the parties and sustain the patent where consistent with the specification and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims construed by reference to the specification, drawings, and state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is to be construed liberally by the specifications, drawings, and state of the art to determine its true scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, claims should be construed to sustain all that the patentee has invented; construction should be such as persons skilled in the art would give, using specification and drawings to interpret ambiguous claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor: court decides construction (law); jury decides application to facts (fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of the patent is for the court as a matter of law, while its application to the facts (e.g., whether an accused device falls within that construction) is for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court should explain the patent's meaning and the jury should examine the evidence of fact under that legal construction; the court need not submit construction questions to the jury unless requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent language must be applied as persons skilled in the art would understand it
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing patents the court should interpret the instrument as persons skilled in the art would, applying its words to its subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical meaning and the inventor's intended use are relevant; courts should remember that specification and claims are often unskilfully drafted and should interpret them in light of the art so as to effectuate the invention rather than defeat it.
